links.note: 1131 has the man say that for those worn down by love there is no strength that is a safeguard (ஏமம்) except the palmyra horse (மடலல்லது இல்லை வலி). In 1164 the woman says the sea of love exists but the safe raft to swim it does not (ஏமப் புணைமன்னும் இல்). The one ஏமம் he names is a man's recourse; her verse shows a sufferer for whom even that is missing.

1131 calls the palmyra horse the only safeguard for those who suffer in love. 1137 praises womanhood that suffers a sea of desire (கடலன்ன காமம் உழந்தும்) and still does not mount it (மடலேறா). The same verb உழந்து marks the same suffering, so 1137 limits 1131: the remedy is one a woman forgoes, and forgoing it is counted as worth.

In 1132 the body and life that cannot bear it (நோனா உடம்பும் உயிரும்) will mount the palmyra horse, setting shame aside (நாணினை நீக்கி நிறுத்து). In 1163 love and shame hang balanced, with life as the carrying pole, inside 'my body that cannot bear' (நோனா உடம்பின் அகத்து). The same three terms, unbearing body, life and shame, appear in both: he ends the strain by dropping shame, she goes on carrying both loads.

In 1247 the woman tells her heart to give up either desire or shame, since she cannot bear the two together (காமம் விடு ஒன்றோ நாண்விடு). 1132 is that choice made: the man keeps desire and puts shame aside (நாணினை நீக்கி) to ride the palmyra horse. Read together, 1247 states the dilemma and 1132 shows one way out of it.

1017 says those ruled by shame give up life for shame and do not give up shame for life's sake (உயிர்ப்பொருட்டால் நாண்துறவார்). In 1132 the man's body and life, unable to endure, put shame aside (நாணினை நீக்கி) and mount the palmyra horse. They conflict only if the lover's speech is read as a claim about what one should do; taken as a dramatised speech it is an instance of exactly what 1017 says the நாணாள்பவர் never do.

In 1133 the man says he once had shame and good manliness (நாணொடு நல்லாண்மை பண்டுடையேன்) and today has the palmyra horse. In 1254 the woman says she used to say she had restraint (நிறையுடையேன் என்பேன்மன்), yet her desire passes concealment and comes out in public. Each speaker sets a former self-possession against its loss to love; his loss is நாண் and ஆண்மை, hers is நிறை.

In 1088 the man, on first seeing her, says his might (பீடு), which enemies dreaded in battle, has broken before her bright forehead. In 1133 he says the shame and good manliness he once had are replaced by the palmyra horse. The later verse carries the first collapse through to its end: what broke at first sight is now given up publicly.

1026 defines நல்லாண்மை as making oneself fit to manage the house one was born into (இல்லாண்மை ஆக்கிக் கொளல்). 1133 uses the same word for what the lover had before (நல்லாண்மை பண்டுடையேன்) and has now exchanged for the palmyra horse. Set beside 1026's definition, the lover's loss is of the capacity that makes a man of use to his family, not only of pride.

1134 says the fierce flood of love (காமக் கடும்புனல்) carries off the raft of shame and good manliness. In 1167 the woman swims the same காமக் கடும்புனல் and sees no shore. The phrase is identical: the man loses his raft to the flood, and the woman is in it with no raft and no bank in sight.

1134 has the flood of love carry away the raft called shame and good manliness (நாணொடு நல்லாண்மை என்னும் புணை). 1251 has the axe of desire break the door called restraint, bolted with the bar of shame (நிறையென்னும் நாணுத்தாழ் வீழ்த்த கதவு). Both make shame a built defence that love's force destroys, one in the man's voice and one in the woman's.

306 says anger burns the safe raft that is one's own people (இனமென்னும் ஏமப் புணையைச் சுடும்). 1134 says the flood of love sweeps off the raft that is shame and good manliness (என்னும் புணை). In both a passion destroys the thing figured as the raft that keeps a person afloat: anger in the chapter on not being angry, desire here.

In 1135 the man says the girl with small bangles gave him (தந்தாள்) the palmyra horse and the grief that evening brings. In 1183 the woman says he took her grace and shame and gave in return (கைம்மாறா ... தந்து) sickness and pallor. Each lover describes the affliction as a gift from the other, and in both verses shame is part of what is lost.

1135 speaks of the grief endured at evening (மாலை உழக்கும் துயர்). 1227 says this sickness buds in the morning, is in bud all day and blossoms in the evening (மாலை மலரும் இந்நோய்). Parimelazhagar explains 1135's 'evening' by the same idea, that love opens at evening, so 1227 supplies the reason behind the man's phrase.

In 1136 the man's eyes will not close (படல் ஒல்லா) for the girl, so even at midnight (யாமத்தும்) he thinks of riding the palmyra horse. In 1252 the woman says desire, having no pity, rules her heart at its work even at midnight (யாமத்தும் ஆளும் தொழில்). Both use midnight, when all else rests, as the proof that love allows no rest.

1049 says one may sleep even in fire, but in poverty closing the eyes at all is hard (யாதொன்றும் கண்பாடு அரிது). 1136 says the lover's eyes will not close (படல் ஒல்லா ... கண்) even at midnight. The Kural gives sleeplessness the same role in two domains: it is the measure of want in the Book of Wealth and of love here.

54 asks what is of greater worth than a woman, if she has the firmness called கற்பு (பெண்ணின் பெருந்தக்க யாவுள). 1137 says nothing is of greater worth than womanhood that suffers a sea of desire and does not mount the palmyra horse (பெண்ணின் பெருந்தக்கது இல்). The wording is reused almost exactly: the Book of Virtue rests her worth on firmness as a wife, the Book of Love on restraint under desire.

907 says a woman who has shame holds more greatness than the manhood of one who does a woman's bidding (நாணுடைப் பெண்ணே பெருமை உடைத்து). 1137 gives the highest worth to womanhood that does not ride the palmyra horse, in a chapter where the man gives up shame and manliness (1133). Both rank a woman who keeps her shame above a man who has let his go.

1138 says love, without thinking 'they are hard to overcome in restraint' or 'they deserve pity', passes concealment and comes out in the open (மறையிறந்து மன்று படும்). 1254 ends with the same words, after the woman says she used to claim she had restraint (நிறையுடையேன் என்பேன்). The shared line is stated generally in 1138 and as a personal confession in 1254; both set நிறை against it and lose.

71 asks whether there is a bolt that can shut love in (அன்பிற்கும் உண்டோ அடைக்குந்தாழ்), since the small tears of the loving make it known. 1138 says காமம் breaks through secrecy and appears in public. The Book of Virtue says of அன்பு what the Book of Love says of காமம்: neither can be kept hidden, and each publishes itself.

In 1139 the woman's love, thinking 'not everyone knows' (அறிகிலார் எல்லாரும் என்றே), goes reeling through the street (மறுகின் மறுகும்). In 1180 she says the town easily learns the secret of those whose eyes are beaten drums (அறைபறை கண்ணார்). In both the secret is given away by the lover herself and not by the town: by her love going about in 1139, by her eyes in 1180.

In 1140 the woman says the unknowing laugh where she can see, because they have not undergone what she has (யாம்பட்ட தாம்படா ஆறு). In 1219 she says those who blame him for not being gracious in waking life are those who have not seen a lover in dreams (காதலர்க் காணாதவர்). Both explain the town's judgement by its lack of the lover's experience.

877 advises not telling one's pain to those who do not know it (நோவற்க நொந்தது அறியார்க்கு). 1140 shows the reason from inside: those who have not suffered what the speaker suffered (யாம்பட்ட தாம்படா) laugh at her in plain sight. The statecraft maxim and the lover's complaint agree that pain gets no hearing from those who have not felt it.

1141 says that because gossip has risen the precious life holds on (அலரெழ ஆருயிர் நிற்கும்). 1213 says the woman's life exists because she sees in dreams the one who gives nothing in waking life (காண்டலின் உண்டென் உயிர்). In each a lover's life is kept going by something that only stands in for the beloved: the town's talk in one, a dream in the other.

1141 says life stays because the gossip has risen. 1263 says the woman still exists by longing for his return (வரல்நசைஇ இன்னும் உளேன்). Both verses name the one thing that keeps life from leaving; in 1141 it comes from outside, from the town, and in 1263 from her own hope.

In 1142 the man says the town, not knowing how hard the flower-eyed woman is to reach (அருமை அறியாது), has given him gossip (அலரெமக்கு ஈந்தது). In 1150 the speaker says the town is raising the very talk 'we want' (யாம்வேண்டும் கெளவை எடுக்கும் இவ்வூர்). Both treat the town's gossip as an unintended service; Parimelazhagar reads ஈந்தது as help given, and reads 1150 as the friend counting on it.

In 1143 the man says the gossip the town knows is like having obtained what he has not obtained (பெறாஅது பெற்றன்ன நீர்த்து). In 1213 the woman sees in dreams the man who gives nothing in waking life, and lives by it. Both take a substitute for union as if it were union: public talk for him, a dream for her.

In 1144 the man says his love thrives through gossip (கவ்வையால் கவ்விது காமம்) and without it would lose its nature and go slack. In 1147 the woman says the town's gossip is manure and her mother's words water to 'this sickness' (நீளும் இந்நோய்). Both say gossip feeds love; he calls what grows காமம் and welcomes it, she calls it நோய்.

1145 says love is sweeter each time it is exposed, as drinking is desired each time one is drunk (களித்தொறும் கள்ளுண்டல் வேட்டற்றால்). 940 says life is loved more each time it suffers, as gambling is loved more with each loss (இழத்தொறூஉம் காதலிக்கும் சூதேபோல்). The two verses have the same shape, a 'each time ... the more' simile from a vice, applied to love in one and to attachment to life in the other.

1145 takes drinking as the model for love: each exposure makes love sweeter as each bout makes drink wanted. 1281 says being intoxicated at a thought and glad at a sight belong to love and not to liquor (கள்ளுக்கில் காமத்திற்கு உண்டு). So the likeness in 1145 has a limit the book itself states: liquor works only when drunk, love without contact.

1110 says that as each new knowing shows one's earlier ignorance (அறிதோறு அறியாமை கண்டற்றால்), so is love each time one draws close to her (செறிதோறும்). 1145 says love is sweeter each time it comes out (வெளிப்படுந் தோறும் இனிது). Both use the தோறும் construction to say love increases with each repetition, in union in 1110 and in exposure in 1145.

In 1146 the woman saw him one day only, and the gossip has spread like the serpent seizing the moon (திங்களைப் பாம்புகொண்டற்று), which Parimelazhagar glosses as spreading everywhere. 957 says a fault in the well-born shows high, like the spot on the moon in the sky (மதிக்கண் மறுப்போல்). Both use the moon as the thing whose blemish everyone sees: a brief event or a small fault becomes public because of where it sits.

In 1147 the woman says the town's gossip is manure (எருவாக) and her mother's word water (நீராக) by which this sickness grows. In 1144 the man says his love thrives by gossip and would go slack without it. The claim is the same from both lovers, but she counts her mother's rebuke with the gossip and calls the growth a sickness.

1147 makes the sickness of love a crop, manured by gossip and watered by a mother's words, that grows long (நீளும் இந்நோய்). 1227 makes the same இந்நோய் a flower that buds in the morning and opens in the evening. In both the woman describes her lovesickness as a plant with its own growth, fed in 1147 and timed in 1227.

1038, on farming, says manuring is better than ploughing and guarding better than watering (எருவிடுதல் ... நீரினும்). 1147 uses the same pair, எரு and நீர், for the gossip and the mother's words that raise the sickness of love. The farmer's two inputs are turned into a figure: what is meant to check the love is what cultivates it.

1148 says that to think of putting out love with gossip is like thinking to put out fire with ghee (நெய்யால் எரி நுதுப்பேம்). 1260 asks whether those whose hearts are like fat put in fire (நிணம் தீயில் இட்டன்ன) can say they will hold out in a sulk. Both use fat meeting fire for love: in 1148 the fat feeds the fire, in 1260 the heart is the fat that melts.

1144 says love thrives by gossip and would droop without it. 1148 puts the same point as a rebuttal of those who expect gossip to end the affair: it is ghee on fire. 1148 gives the image and the opposing view that 1144's plain statement lacks.

In 1154 the woman asks whether, if he who was gracious and said 'do not fear' should leave (அளித்தஞ்சல் என்றவர் நீப்பின்), any fault lies with her for trusting his assurance. In 1149 the one who said 'do not fear' has left (அஞ்சலோம்பு என்றார் ... நீத்தக் கடை), and she asks how she can now be ashamed of gossip. The same promise is quoted before and after it is broken: the fear of 1154 has come true in 1149.

In 1149 the woman asks whether she can be ashamed at gossip (அலர்நாண ஒல்வதோ) now that he has left her. In 1297 she says she has forgotten even shame (நாணும் மறந்தேன்), caught in a heart that cannot forget him. In both her shame gives way, in 1149 because his leaving has made it pointless and in 1297 because her own heart overrides it.

1150 says the town is raising the gossip 'we want' (யாம்வேண்டும் கெளவை), and the lover will grant what is asked if he wishes. In 1143 the man asks whether the gossip the town knows is not his to have, since it is like gaining what he has not gained. Both sides welcome the talk: for him it stands in for union, and in 1150, on Parimelazhagar's reading, it is the ground for asking him to take her away.
